questions.prompt: In the standard DBMS layering, which component decides between an index scan and a sequential scan for a given query?
options: The cost-based optimizer inside the query processor, using table statistics.
The buffer manager, based on which pages are currently resident.
The storage engine's access method, at the moment of the first read.
The transport layer, based on the client's connection settings.
questions.explanation: Plan selection is the optimizer's job: it estimates costs from statistics gathered by ANALYZE and chooses, for example, an Index Scan over a Seq Scan. The execution and storage engines merely run the chosen plan.

questions.prompt: Why is a storage engine described as swappable behind the execution engine?
options: The execution engine talks to it through a narrow cursor API (open, seek, next, insert, commit), so InnoDB, RocksDB, or WiredTiger can be substituted.
Because the SQL standard fully specifies the on-disk format, any engine is byte-compatible.
Because all storage engines share one buffer pool defined by the DBMS core.
Because the optimizer emits engine-specific machine code at plan time.
questions.explanation: The engine sits behind a narrow record/cursor interface, which is exactly why MySQL can swap InnoDB/MyRocks and MongoDB moved to WiredTiger. The SQL standard deliberately leaves the storage format unspecified.

questions.prompt: How does a running PostgreSQL instance handle client connections?
options: The postmaster forks a dedicated backend process per connection, all attached to a shared-memory buffer pool.
A single-threaded event loop multiplexes all connections over epoll.
A fixed thread pool inside one process serves connections round-robin.
Each connection gets its own private copy of the entire database cache.
questions.explanation: Postgres is process-per-connection: the postmaster forks one backend per client, and all backends attach to shared memory (shared_buffers, WAL buffers, lock tables). This is why a pooler like PgBouncer is needed at scale.

questions.prompt: What is `shared_buffers` in PostgreSQL?
options: The shared-memory buffer pool that every backend attaches to, so a page cached by one backend is visible to all.
A per-backend private read cache that is discarded when the session ends.
The on-disk write-ahead log segment directory.
The temporary space used only for sorting and hashing during query execution.
questions.explanation: shared_buffers is a fixed region of shared memory serving as the buffer pool; because backends are separate processes, sharing the cache requires it to live in shared memory with explicit lightweight locks.

questions.prompt: What fundamentally distinguishes a disk-based DBMS from an in-memory DBMS?
options: Where the authoritative copy of the data lives; disk-based uses RAM as a cache, in-memory holds the primary copy in RAM.
Whether the database supports SQL; in-memory systems are always key-value.
Whether the system is durable; in-memory systems can never survive a crash.
Whether indexes are used; in-memory systems never build indexes.
questions.explanation: The distinction is the location of the authoritative copy, driven by the ~100 ns / ~50-100 us / ~10 ms gap between DRAM, NVMe, and disk. Disk-based engines use on-disk structures that minimize block transfers; in-memory engines can use pointer-rich structures.

questions.prompt: Why can't an on-disk structure store ordinary memory pointers between records?
options: The file is mapped at different addresses across runs, so records are addressed by page id + offset instead.
Pointers are larger than 8 bytes on disk and waste too much space.
The block device firmware rewrites any value that looks like a pointer.
The SQL standard forbids pointer storage for portability reasons.
questions.explanation: A stored pointer would be meaningless after restart because the data is not mapped at a fixed address. On-disk structures therefore address data by page id + offset, which shapes all of file formats and B-tree implementation.

questions.prompt: How does an in-memory store such as Redis achieve durability despite RAM being volatile?
options: A write-ahead log (append + fsync) plus periodic snapshots; recovery loads the latest snapshot and replays the log suffix.
By mirroring every write synchronously to a second RAM-only replica.
By relying on ECC memory to retain contents through a power loss.
It cannot be durable; any crash loses all committed data by design.
questions.explanation: Redis uses AOF (the write-ahead log) plus RDB (snapshots). Durability is a knob (appendfsync always/everysec/no), independent of the storage medium: an in-memory store can be fully durable and a disk store can lose data.

questions.prompt: What does group commit trade off?
options: It batches many writes per fsync, accepting a bounded loss window for much higher throughput.
It commits each write with two fsyncs to double durability at half the speed.
It disables the WAL entirely to remove all sync overhead.
It replicates commits to a quorum before acknowledging any single write.
questions.explanation: Because an fsync costs tens to hundreds of microseconds, flushing per write caps throughput at the device's sync rate. Group commit amortizes one fsync over many writes, trading a small potential-loss window for throughput.

questions.prompt: Why does a column-oriented layout win at analytical (OLAP) queries?
options: I/O is proportional to the columns touched, compression is far better, and execution can be vectorized with SIMD.
It stores each whole row contiguously, so a single-row read is one access.
It avoids indexes entirely, so every query is a fast hash probe.
It keeps all data in memory, so disk layout is irrelevant.
questions.explanation: A query over a few of many columns reads only those columns; adjacent same-type values compress dramatically (RLE, dictionary, delta); and dense typed arrays enable batched SIMD execution. The cost is expensive single-row insert/update.

questions.prompt: Why is a column store poor at OLTP single-row operations?
options: Inserting or reading one row touches every column's storage separately, scattering the work across N locations.
Column stores cannot enforce primary keys, so single-row lookups are ambiguous.
Each column is encrypted independently, making row assembly impossible.
Column stores lack a buffer pool, so every row read hits disk.
questions.explanation: Because each column is stored contiguously and separately, a single-row insert becomes N appends and a single-row read gathers N scattered values back into a tuple. Point updates are especially costly, which is why column stores are usually append-mostly.

questions.prompt: What carries the MVCC visibility information in a PostgreSQL heap tuple?
options: The xmin/xmax transaction ids and the t_ctid pointer in the tuple header.
A per-page bitmap stored in the page footer.
The primary-key B-tree leaf entry that points at the tuple.
A separate visibility file maintained by the WAL writer.
questions.explanation: xmin/xmax record the inserting and deleting transactions, and t_ctid links to the next version of the row. Postgres never overwrites in place on update; both versions coexist and visibility rules pick the right one, which is why VACUUM is needed.

questions.prompt: How is a tuple addressed within a PostgreSQL heap, and why the extra indirection?
options: By TID = (page number, line-pointer index); the line pointer lets tuples move within a page without updating any index.
By a raw 64-bit byte offset into the table file, updated in every index on any move.
By the primary-key value, which every secondary index also stores.
By a hash of the row contents, recomputed on each update.
questions.explanation: A tuple's TID is (page, line-pointer index), exposed as ctid. Indexes point at the line pointer, not raw bytes, so intra-page compaction only moves tuples and rewrites line pointers, leaving index entries valid.

questions.prompt: How would you get columnar analytics from PostgreSQL?
options: Use a columnar table access method (Citus columnar), a Parquet foreign data wrapper, or pair it with an embedded column engine like DuckDB.
Add a B-tree index on every column and enable index-only scans.
Set shared_buffers larger than the table so the whole heap is cached.
Run VACUUM FULL to rewrite the heap in column order.
questions.explanation: Core Postgres is a row store; columnar comes from outside the heap via the pluggable table-AM (Citus columnar), foreign data wrappers over Parquet, or an external engine like DuckDB. You cannot turn a row store columnar with an index.

questions.prompt: What is a zone map (per-block min/max metadata) used for in a column store?
options: Skipping entire column blocks whose value range cannot satisfy a query predicate.
Encrypting each block with a per-zone key.
Mapping logical row numbers to physical disk sectors.
Tracking which transactions have read each block for MVCC.
questions.explanation: Per-block min/max statistics let the engine prune whole blocks (row groups / granules) that cannot match a predicate, reading far less data. It is the same sparse-index idea used by B-tree internal levels.

questions.prompt: How does vectorized execution differ from the classic Volcano/iterator model?
options: It returns a batch of values per next() call, amortizing dispatch and enabling SIMD, instead of one tuple per call.
It stores data in columns rather than rows on disk.
It compiles the entire query to machine code before running it.
It runs each operator on a separate thread for parallelism.
questions.explanation: Volcano execution pulls one tuple per next() per operator, costing a virtual call per tuple. Vectorized execution processes batches (e.g. 1024 values), amortizing dispatch and enabling SIMD. It is independent of on-disk layout, though it pairs well with columns.

questions.prompt: What is PAX (Partition Attributes Across)?
options: Store row groups, but lay columns out contiguously within each group, blending columnar scans with row locality.
A protocol for partitioning a table across multiple nodes.
A replication mode that ships column deltas to replicas.
A lock-escalation policy that groups row locks into page locks.
questions.explanation: PAX keeps a group of rows together but stores each column contiguously within the group, gaining columnar compression and scan behavior while keeping a group's data local. Parquet and ORC are essentially PAX; the Postgres heap is not.

questions.prompt: Why is it incorrect to call Cassandra or HBase 'column-oriented'?
options: 'Wide-column' names a data model (a sparse map of maps in column families); physically they are usually LSM engines, not a compressed columnar format.
They are actually pure row stores identical to PostgreSQL's heap.
They store data only in memory, so on-disk orientation is undefined.
They are graph databases, not tabular stores at all.
questions.explanation: Wide-column refers to the data model: a row key maps to column families, each a possibly per-row-variable set of columns. The physical engine is typically LSM-tree, not the compressed columnar layout of ClickHouse or Vertica.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of an index file relative to a data file?
options: It maps a search key to a location in the data file, turning an O(N) scan into an O(log N) or O(1) lookup.
It stores a compressed backup copy of the data file for recovery.
It holds the write-ahead log records for the table.
It caches query results so repeated queries skip the data file.
questions.explanation: Data files hold records; index files map keys to record locations so lookups are sublinear. Without indexes, every point query would be a full sequential scan of the table.

questions.prompt: What does a secondary index store at its leaves in InnoDB's clustered (index-organized) tables?
options: The primary key value, which is then used to descend the clustered B-tree to the row.
A physical byte offset directly into a heap file.
The full row image, duplicated from the clustered index.
A TID identical to PostgreSQL's (page, line-pointer) pair.
questions.explanation: Because rows live in the clustered PK B-tree and can move on page splits, secondary indexes store the PK rather than a physical pointer. So a secondary lookup does two descents, and a large PK bloats every secondary index.

questions.prompt: How is a PostgreSQL table physically organized with respect to its primary key?
options: Heap-organized: rows sit in an unordered heap and the primary key is just a unique B-tree pointing via TID; no clustered order is maintained.
Index-organized: the table is a B-tree keyed on the primary key with full rows in the leaves.
Hash-organized: rows are bucketed by a hash of the primary key.
Sorted: the heap is continuously kept in primary-key order.
questions.explanation: Postgres is heap-organized; the primary key is an ordinary unique B-tree index pointing at TIDs. CLUSTER reorders the heap once and the order then decays; Postgres maintains no clustered index.

questions.prompt: How many clustered indexes can a table have, and why?
options: At most one, because the data can be physically ordered by only one key.
Exactly one per column, since each column can be clustered independently.
Unlimited, because clustering is just metadata on the index.
None, because clustering is a query-time decision, not a storage property.
questions.explanation: Clustered means index order equals data order, and data can only be laid out one way, so there is at most one clustered index. All other indexes are non-clustered and independent of the data's physical order.

questions.prompt: Why must a PostgreSQL index-only scan still consult the visibility map?
options: MVCC visibility information lives in the heap, so a not-all-visible page forces a heap fetch even when the index covers the query.
The index does not store column values, only keys, so data must be re-read.
The visibility map holds the actual column data for covered queries.
Index-only scans are disabled unless the visibility map is empty.
questions.explanation: A covering index can answer from its leaves, but because tuple visibility (xmin/xmax) is in the heap, Postgres checks the visibility map; if the page is not marked all-visible, it must fetch the heap tuple to judge visibility.

questions.prompt: What is a HOT (Heap-Only Tuple) update in PostgreSQL?
options: An update that fits on the same page and changes no indexed column, chaining the new version via t_ctid and touching no index.
An update that rewrites every index entry to point at the new tuple version.
An in-memory update that never reaches the heap until checkpoint.
An update applied directly to the WAL without modifying the heap page.
questions.explanation: When the new version fits on the same page and no indexed column changed, Postgres links it off the old tuple via t_ctid and updates no index, relying entirely on the line-pointer indirection. HOT greatly reduces index write amplification.

questions.prompt: Why does PostgreSQL require VACUUM?
options: MVCC leaves old tuple versions as dead tuples in the heap; VACUUM reclaims them and their index entries, preventing bloat and XID wraparound.
It defragments the WAL so replay after a crash is faster.
It rebuilds the buffer pool cache after a restart.
It compresses column data to reclaim disk space.
questions.explanation: Every update/delete writes a new version and leaves the old as a dead tuple. VACUUM (and autovacuum) reclaim dead tuples and their index entries; neglect causes table bloat and eventually transaction-ID wraparound that forces the database read-only.

questions.prompt: What are the three orthogonal axes that define a storage structure?
options: Buffering (batch writes or not), mutability (in-place vs append-only), and ordering (sorted by key or not).
Consistency, availability, and partition tolerance.
Read latency, write latency, and network latency.
Isolation level, lock granularity, and replication factor.
questions.explanation: Nearly every engine is defined by these three choices. B-trees are unbuffered/in-place/ordered; LSM trees are buffered/immutable/ordered. The axes predict the performance profile, which is why they organize all of Part I.

questions.prompt: Express the B-tree vs LSM-tree trade-off in terms of the three axes.
options: B-trees are in-place/ordered/mostly-unbuffered (great reads, random writes); LSM trees are buffered/immutable/ordered (great writes, at the cost of read and space amplification).
B-trees are append-only and unordered; LSM trees are in-place and sorted.
Both are identical on disk and differ only in their query language.
B-trees buffer writes in a memtable; LSM trees mutate pages in place.
questions.explanation: B-trees mutate pages in place and keep keys ordered, giving excellent point/range reads but random write I/O. LSM trees buffer writes in a memtable and flush immutable sorted SSTables, giving high write throughput at the cost of read/space amplification and compaction (the RUM-conjecture trade).

questions.prompt: Trace a point lookup `SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = 42` through PostgreSQL. What is the correct order?
options: Parse/catalog-resolve, optimizer picks an Index Scan, B-tree descent yields a TID, heap page fetched via the buffer pool, MVCC visibility applied, tuple returned.
Sequential scan of the heap, filter each row, return the first match, then update statistics.
Hash the id, probe a hash table in shared memory, and return the row with no disk access.
Read the WAL to find the latest version of row 42, then acknowledge to the client.
questions.explanation: The backend parses and resolves the query, the optimizer chooses an Index Scan on the pkey, the B-tree is descended (pages via the buffer pool) to a TID, the heap page is fetched and the line pointer followed, MVCC visibility is checked (following the t_ctid chain if needed), and the visible tuple is returned.
